short: PRDM proteins are zinc-finger transcription factors defined by an N-terminal PR domain, a variant of the SET methyltransferase fold, followed by a tandem array of C2H2 zinc fingers that does the DNA binding. The family is heterogeneous and does not share one motif: each member's finger array reads its own sequence, and those sequences are unrelated to one another. The best-characterized members are PRDM1/BLIMP1, which binds an interferon-regulatory-factor-like AAAGTGAAAG site and drives plasma-cell differentiation; PRDM9, whose rapidly evolving finger array selects meiotic recombination hotspots and underlies a mouse hybrid-sterility phenotype; PRDM14, in naive pluripotency; and PRDM16, in brown adipocyte and craniofacial development. A hit labelled PRDM should be interpreted per member, never as a family-level call.
long:
## The factors

The PRDM proteins take their name from the PR domain, a diverged SET domain of about 130 residues,
followed by a variable number of C2H2 zinc fingers [PMID:22669819]. Humans have roughly 19 PRDM genes. This family
groups the ones for which a motif has actually been measured: PRDM1, PRDM4, PRDM5, PRDM6, PRDM9,
PRDM10, PRDM13, PRDM14, PRDM15 and PRDM16. MECOM (historically PRDM3) is kept as a separate family
here because its two zinc-finger clusters behave differently from a single array.

Only some PR domains are catalytically active. PRDM9 is a genuine histone H3 lysine-4
trimethyltransferase, first described in mouse as Meisetz, and that activity is required for meiotic
prophase [PMID:16292313]. For most other members the PR domain has no demonstrated methyltransferase activity and acts
as a protein-interaction surface; PRDM1/BLIMP1, for instance, works by recruiting histone deacetylase
and methyltransferase cofactors rather than by modifying histones itself [PMID:22669819]. Expression is mostly
restricted. PRDM1 appears in plasma cells, effector T cells, keratinocytes, primordial germ cells and
placenta; PRDM9 essentially only in meiotic germ cells; PRDM14 in embryonic stem cells and germ cells;
PRDM16 in brown and beige adipocytes, craniofacial mesenchyme and hematopoietic stem cells. Few PRDMs
are broadly expressed, so the plausible member behind a hit is usually decided by cell type rather than
by sequence.

## The motif

There is no family consensus, and the data in this atlas show that plainly: member motifs range from the
GTTTCAAG core of PRDM4, through the IRF-like AAAGTGAAAG of PRDM1, to GGTCTCTAAC for PRDM14 and G-rich
models for PRDM9 and PRDM16. Cohesion across the family is low, about 0.5, and the medoid motif
(ACTTTCACT, the PRDM1 site on the reverse strand) is simply the most central member, not a shared
element.

PRDM1/BLIMP1 is the clearest case. Its zinc fingers read an approximately 10-bp site built on a GAAAG
core; the optimal selected sequence is close to AAAGTGAAAG, which overlaps a subset of
interferon-stimulated response elements, so BLIMP1 and IRF1/IRF2 compete for the same DNA with
comparable affinities [PMID:15494505]. In vivo, several motif variants are needed to capture BLIMP1 occupancy, and
binding is sensitive to CpG methylation [PMID:20421211]. The reverse-complement rendering ACTTTCACTTT is the same site
and is what several database entries display.

PRDM9 is different in kind. Its DNA-binding module is a minisatellite-encoded tandem array of roughly a
dozen C2H2 fingers, one of the fastest-evolving coding sequences in mammals, polymorphic within humans
and between mouse strains [PMID:20044539]. Human hotspots are enriched for a degenerate 13-mer, CCNCCNTNNCCNC, which
the common human A allele recognizes [PMID:19165926,20044539]; crystal structures of the human PRDM9 finger array on DNA explain
the base contacts, and the C allele reads a different sequence [PMID:26833727]. Because the array differs between
alleles, no single PRDM9 matrix is correct for all individuals, and the JASPAR and CIS-BP PRDM9 models
are approximations of one allele's preference at best.

## Where it acts

PRDM1 sites sit in promoters of genes it represses, including IRF-dependent immune programs, in both
CpG-poor and CpG-island promoters, with the methylation-sensitive variants biased to the latter [PMID:20421211]. PRDM9
sites are the defining feature of meiotic double-strand-break hotspots: tens of thousands of them,
typically 1-2 kb wide, mostly outside promoters, and in mouse directed away from functional elements
such as transcription start sites. PRDM14 and PRDM15 sites are concentrated at enhancers and promoters
of pluripotency and signaling genes in stem cells. PRDM16 sites are found at brown-fat enhancers, where
PRDM16 acts less as an autonomous sequence reader than as a partner of adipogenic factors [PMID:18719582], which matters
for interpreting its ChIP-derived motif.

## Biology and disease

PRDM1 knockout blocks plasma-cell formation and specification of primordial germ cells; in humans PRDM1
is inactivated by mutation and deletion in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, where it behaves as a tumor
suppressor [PMID:16492805]. PRDM9-null mice are sterile with arrested meiosis [PMID:16292313]; PRDM9 allele identity changes hotspot
usage in human families [PMID:20044539]; and one PRDM9 allele is the mouse hybrid-sterility gene, with sterility
reversible by swapping the finger array [PMID:26840484]. PRDM14 loss destabilizes naive pluripotency and PRDM15 loss
does the same through WNT and MAPK-ERK targets. PRDM16 loss impairs brown-fat identity [PMID:18719582], and PRDM16 mutations found in nonsyndromic
left ventricular noncompaction and dilated cardiomyopathy were proposed to cause the cardiomyopathy of
1p36 deletion syndrome [PMID:23768516], an attribution others consider unlikely [PMID:24387995]; PRDM5 loss-of-function causes brittle cornea syndrome [PMID:21664999]; PRDM6
variants cause nonsyndromic patent ductus arteriosus [PMID:27181681]. PRDM10 and PRDM16 also appear as fusion partners
in soft-tissue tumors and leukemia.

## Reading a hit

Treat a PRDM hit as a hit on one named member. Sequence cannot tell you which PRDM bound, because the
members do not share a motif and the family label spans unrelated sites. Check which member the
underlying matrix is labelled with, then whether that member is expressed in your cell type. For PRDM1
the site is short and IRF-like, so an IRF or ISRE explanation is at least as likely as BLIMP1 unless
BLIMP1 is present [PMID:15494505,20421211]. For PRDM9 a match is meaningless outside meiotic germ cells, and allele-dependent
even there. Several PRDM entries rest on ChIP-only evidence, where the motif may belong to a partner;
the EBF-like HOCOMOCO PRDM16 model (PRD16.H14CORE.0.P.B) is one. The HOCOMOCO PRDM13 model, which
matches a SNAI-type CAGGTG E-box, is not: PRD13.H14CORE.0.PSGI.A adds HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq
to ChIP-seq at grade A, so indirect binding does not explain it. Both are flagged as inconsistent with
their labels by their nearest neighbours across databases.
caveats: This family has no shared motif, so a family-level hit means little; only the member-specific matrix matters. Cohesion across members is about 0.5, and two entries contradict their labels: the HOCOMOCO PRDM16 model (TCCCCTGGGA) resembles an EBF site and rests on ChIP-seq alone, where a partner motif is the simpler explanation, while the PRDM13 model (GCAGGTGG) is a SNAI-type E-box despite grade-A in vitro support, so it is either a genuine E-box-like preference or a mislabel. PRDM1 evidence is strong and includes in vitro selection, but the site overlaps IRF elements, so IRF1, IRF2 or an ISRE is a competing interpretation. PRDM9 matrices describe one allele of a polymorphic finger array and are interpretable only in meiotic germ cells. Short G-rich PRDM models match frequently by chance.

timeline.finding: PRDI-BF1, a five-zinc-finger protein, is identified as a repressor that binds the PRDI element of the human interferon-beta promoter and is proposed to act by displacing its activators.
timeline.methods: Sequence-specific binding to PRDI; cotransfection reporter assays
timeline.open: The binding site was known only as PRDI; its relation to IRF sites and to B-cell differentiation was not yet recognized.

timeline.finding: Mouse Blimp-1, the orthologue of PRDI-BF1, is cloned as a zinc-finger factor induced in, and able to drive, the maturation of B cells into immunoglobulin-secreting cells.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; transfection of B-lymphoma lines
timeline.open: Its DNA-binding specificity had not been defined.

timeline.finding: The optimal BLIMP1 site is determined and found to match the subset of IRF sites containing GAAAG; BLIMP1, IRF1 and IRF2 bind such sites with similar affinities and compete at the IFNB promoter.
timeline.methods: In vitro site selection; EMSA competition and dissociation constants; ChIP; cotransfection
timeline.open: How many genomic BLIMP1 sites are shared with IRFs was unknown.

timeline.finding: Meisetz (PRDM9) is shown to be a histone H3 lysine-4 trimethyltransferase expressed only in germ cells entering meiotic prophase; knockout mice of both sexes are sterile.
timeline.methods: Histone methyltransferase assays; gene knockout in mouse
timeline.open: What targets PRDM9 to particular sites in the genome was not addressed.

timeline.finding: A degenerate 13-mer, CCNCCNTNNCCNC, is found to recruit crossovers to at least 40% of human recombination hotspots.
timeline.methods: Population-genetic hotspot maps (HapMap Phase 2); motif enrichment
timeline.open: The protein that reads the 13-mer was unknown.

timeline.finding: PRDM9 is identified as the major determinant of hotspot location: the human consensus allele is predicted, and shown in vitro, to bind the 13-mer, and PRDM9 finger-array alleles track hotspot usage in mice and humans.
timeline.methods: Mouse strain genetics; zinc-finger recognition prediction; in vitro binding; human association
timeline.open: Because the finger array is highly polymorphic, a single matrix could describe only one allele.

timeline.finding: Genome-wide BLIMP1 promoter occupancy shows that several motif variants are needed to capture its specificity, that binding is methylation-sensitive, and that only a subset of occupied sites overlap IRF motifs.
timeline.methods: ChIP-chip; motif discovery and enrichment; knock-down

timeline.finding: A crystal structure of PRDM9 allele A fingers 8-12 on hotspot DNA explains its base contacts and allele-specific affinities, and humanizing the mouse PRDM9 finger array repositions hotspots and restores fertility in sterile hybrids.
timeline.methods: X-ray crystallography; in vitro binding of allelic variants; humanized-allele mouse genetics
timeline.open: Why symmetric binding of both homologues is needed for fertility remains mechanistically unexplained.

open: Whether PRDM16 loss causes the cardiomyopathy of 1p36 deletion syndrome is disputed: Arndt et al. (2013) mapped a minimal deletion to PRDM16 and found PRDM16 mutations in noncompaction and dilated cardiomyopathy, while de Leeuw and Houge (2014) argued that PRDM16 loss is unlikely to explain the cardiomyopathy in the deletion syndrome.

The HOCOMOCO PRDM13 model (GCAGGTGG) looks like a SNAI-type E-box, yet it carries in vitro support (HT-SELEX, GHT-SELEX and SMiLE-seq, grade A), so it is unresolved whether PRDM13 genuinely reads an E-box-like site or the model is mislabelled; the EBF-like PRDM16 model, by contrast, rests on ChIP-seq alone, where a partner motif is the simpler explanation.

How PRDM9 binding leads to fertile meiosis is not settled: hotspot position follows the allele's binding specificity, but in hybrid mice fertility tracks whether PRDM9 binds both homologues symmetrically, and the downstream step that requires symmetry is unknown.

Which BLIMP1 sites are direct high-affinity targets and which are competitive IRF-overlapping sites is only partly resolved: in vitro selection gives one AAAGTGAAAG-like site, while promoter occupancy needs several motif variants that differ in CpG content and methylation sensitivity.
